docs.text: HardFOC driver ISF15ACP4 Driver ¶ A C++20 driver for the NKK ISF15ACP4 SmartDisplay, a pushbutton with a 96 x 64 colour OLED in its keytop. It initialises the display's SSD1331 controller, draws text, shapes, images and animations, and reads the switch, on any MCU with SPI. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that writes SPI bytes with the D/C and SS lines, sets the reset and supply-enable pins and reads the switch; it does the rest: the reset pulse, the controller's initialisation table, memory windows, colour conversion and the hardware drawing commands. Frameless OLED pushbutton ISF15ACP4 NKK Switches (SmartDisplay) Display 96 x 64 RGB passive-matrix OLED, 65,536 colours (RGB565), driver with 96 x 64 x 16-bit display RAM Host interface SPI, write only: SS, D/C, SCK, SDI; clock cycle 150 ns minimum (about 6.6 MHz) Supplies VDD 2.4 V to 3.5 V (logic), VCC 14 V to 16 V (OLED drive, 11 mA typical with all pixels on) Switch SPST normally open, 100 mA at 12 V DC, 2.0 N, 1.8 mm travel, 1,000,000 operations Operating range −20 °C to +70 °C; display life 50,000 h at 100 cd/m² with 40 % of pixels on Driver mode 65k-colour mode; full frames from a CPU canvas, or the controller's line and rectangle commands Datasheet (NKK) What you get ¶ One object per button. SmartDisplay<YourPort> owns the reset, the supply sequence and the SSD1331 initialisation. See API guide . A canvas with text. GraphicsContext draws pixels, lines, rectangles, a 5 x 7 font and RGB565 images into a 12,288-byte frame that Present() uploads. See Graphics . Hardware drawing. Lines, filled rectangles, window clear and scrolling run on the controller with a few command bytes each. See API guide . Animations and a button helper. Animator runs a frame callback at a fixed rate; ButtonUI debounces the switch into press, click and long-press events. See Animations . Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class: no virtual calls, no heap, no RTOS dependency. See Porting . Tested without hardware. Host unit tests check the exact byte stream and pin sequence against a recording port. docs.text: Animations ¶ Run a frame callback at a fixed rate, use the four built-in effects, and draw button feedback with ButtonUI . Snippets on this page are compiled from tests/docs/graphics.cpp . The animator ¶ Animator(gfx, frame_fn, user_data, fps) calls frame_fn(gfx, frame, user_data) each time a frame is due. It keeps no clock of its own: you tell it how much time has passed. void run_plasma ( Display & display , uint32_t ( * millis )()) { auto gfx = display . CreateGraphicsContext (); isf15acp4 :: Animator anim ( gfx , isf15acp4 :: animations :: Plasma , nullptr , 25 ); // 25 FPS: 40 ms per frame uint32_t last = millis (); for (;;) { const uint32_t now = millis (); if ( anim . Tick ( now - last )) { // renders when a frame is due display . Present ( gfx ); } last = now ; } } Member Does Tick(elapsed_ms) Adds the time; when at least one frame period has built up, renders one frame and returns true RenderNow() Renders the next frame at once SetFps(fps) Frame period 1000 / fps ms (33 ms when fps is 0) Frame() , Reset() The frame counter; Reset() sets it and the time to zero Tick() renders at most one frame per call and keeps any extra time, so after a late call the next calls catch up one frame each; no frame number is skipped. The animator only draws: you call Present() when it returns true . Built-in effects ¶ Function Draws ColorWheel A rotating colour wheel, with a label Plasma A moving sine-interference pattern ScrollingText A title and a line of text moving left PulseButton A frame and a growing bar, green when pressed They are in isf15acp4::animations . ColorWheel and Plasma ignore user_data . ScrollingText takes an animations::ScrollTextState* (its text ; null shows "ISF15ACP4"), PulseButton an animations::PulseButtonState* (its pressed ; null is not pressed). ColorWheel and Plasma compute every pixel with floating-point sine functions: on an MCU without an FPU that can take longer than the frame period. Your own effect ¶ A frame function is a plain noexcept function. Pass your state through user_data : struct Bar { uint8_t level ; // 0..95, updated by your code }; void DrawBar ( isf15acp4 :: GraphicsContext & gfx , uint32_t frame , void * user_data ) noexcept { const auto * bar = static_cast < const Bar *> ( user_data ); gfx . Clear ( colors :: Black ); gfx . FillRect ({ 0 , 28 , bar -> level , 36 }, ( frame / 15 ) % 2 ? colors :: Green : colors :: Yellow ); } void start_bar ( isf15acp4 :: GraphicsContext & gfx , Bar & bar ) { isf15acp4 :: Animator anim ( gfx , & DrawBar , & bar , 30 ); anim . RenderNow (); // first frame without waiting } The animator keeps a reference to the context, so the context must outlive it. Button feedback ¶ ButtonUI debounces the switch ( API guide ) and draws two kinds of feedback: isf15acp4 :: ButtonUI ui ; ui . DrawStatus ( gfx , "START" , display . IsPressed ()); // title bar, state text, frame isf15acp4 :: ButtonUI :: DrawGauge ( gfx , 48 , 40 , 20 , load , // half-circle gauge, load in 0..1 colors :: Green , colors :: Gray ); display . Present ( gfx ); Call Draws DrawStatus() A full status screen: title bar with the label, "PRESSED" or "READY", a border DrawGauge() A half disc below its centre, the first value (0 to 1) of it in fg DrawStatus() clears the frame to dark green when active, black otherwise. DrawGauge() is static. The examples combine these: isf15acp4_animation_demo cycles the four effects on each press, and isf15acp4_button_dashboard draws a gauge driven by the switch.

API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: initialise, draw, use the controller's drawing commands, set brightness, read the switch and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Display standing for isf15acp4::SmartDisplay<MySpi> and colors for isf15acp4::colors . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One SmartDisplay<Port> object per button. You draw into a GraphicsContext and hand it to the display; or you call the display's own drawing and window functions, which talk to the controller directly. Task Calls Start Initialize() , Reset() , IsInitialized() Draw a frame CreateGraphicsContext() , then GraphicsContext drawing, then Present() Draw on the controller DrawLine() , DrawRectangle() , ClearWindow() , DrawPixel() , FillScreen() Write pixels yourself SetWindow() , SetFullWindow() , WritePixels() , DrawCanvas() Brightness and power DisplayOn() , DisplayOff() , DisplayDim() , SetMasterCurrent() Scroll ConfigureScroll() Switch IsPressed() , and ButtonUI for events Errors GetLastError() , GetErrorFlags() , HasError() , ClearErrorFlags() Every call that talks to the display returns bool and never throws. Check it: false means a parameter was out of range or the port reported a failure, and an Error flag says which. Initialise ¶ Pick the product variant and graphics backend in SmartDisplayConfig , then call Initialize() : const isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplayConfig config { . variant = isf15acp4 :: ProductVariant :: Isf15acp4 , . graphics = isf15acp4 :: GraphicsBackend :: BuiltinCanvas , . enable_vcc_on_init = true , }; isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplay < MySpi > display ( & spi , config ); return display . Initialize ( config . enable_vcc_on_init ); Initialize() brings the port up, pulses RES, enables VCC (unless you pass false ), sends the variant's initialisation table (which ends with display on) and selects the full window. Reset() runs the same sequence again, for example after a supply brown-out. Configuration lists every field. Draw a frame ¶ auto gfx = display . CreateGraphicsContext (); // holds a 12,288-byte frame: keep it alive gfx . Clear ( colors :: Black ); gfx . FillRect ({ 0 , 0 , 95 , 10 }, colors :: Blue ); gfx . DrawString ( 2 , 2 , "SPINDLE" , colors :: White , colors :: Blue ); char text [ 16 ]; std :: snprintf ( text , sizeof ( text ), "%lu RPM" , static_cast < unsigned long > ( rpm )); gfx . DrawString ( 2 , 24 , text , colors :: Cyan ); return display . Present ( gfx ); // full-window upload Drawing into the context changes RAM on your MCU only; Present() sends the frame as one 12,288-byte data transaction. At 6 MHz that is about 16 ms of SPI time, so a full frame costs at most about 60 frames a second before your drawing time. Text uses the 5 x 7 font, 6 pixels per character: 16 characters across. Graphics covers the backends, colours and images. Draw with the controller ¶ The SSD1331 draws lines and rectangles itself from a few command bytes, which is much less SPI traffic than a frame: if ( ! display . ClearWindow ({ 0 , 0 , 95 , 63 })) { // 25h return false ; } if ( ! display . DrawRectangle ({ 10 , 10 , 85 , 53 }, colors :: Orange , true )) { // 26h fill on, 22h, fill off return false ; } return display . DrawLine ({ 0 , 63 }, { 95 , 0 }, colors :: White ); // 21h Call Command Bytes DrawLine() 21h 8 DrawRectangle() 22h 11 filled 26h , 22h , 26h 17 ClearWindow() 25h 5 DrawPixel() 15h , 75h , data 8 FillScreen() A full frame 12,294 These draw straight into the display RAM. A later Present() overwrites them with the canvas contents. Write pixels yourself ¶ // An 8 x 8 red square at (40, 28): window, then 64 pixels. isf15acp4 :: Color565 block [ 8 * 8 ]; for ( auto & px : block ) { px = colors :: Red ; } if ( ! display . SetWindow ({ 40 , 28 , 47 , 35 })) { // 15h / 75h, inclusive bounds return false ; } if ( ! display . WriteColors ( block , 8 * 8 )) { // high byte first on any CPU return false ; } return display . SetFullWindow (); // back to 96 x 64 for Present() SetWindow() takes inclusive bounds in display coordinates and returns false with Error::OutOfRange outside the visible area (0..95, 0..63 on the ISF15ACP4); on the smaller variants the driver adds the RAM column offset. WriteColors() needs Initialize() first and sends each Color565 pixel high byte first, the SSD1331's 65k-colour order. WritePixels() sends raw bytes unchanged, two per pixel already in that format, and needs an even byte count. Restore the full window before the next Present() ; DrawCanvas() and Present() set it themselves. Brightness and power ¶ if ( ! display . DisplayOff ()) { // AEh: sleep, GRAM kept return false ; } if ( ! display . SetMasterCurrent ( 0x08 )) { // 87h: 0x00 (dimmest) .. 0x0F (brightest) return false ; } if ( ! display . DisplayOn ()) { // AFh: normal display return false ; } return display . DisplayDim (); // ACh: dim mode, for an idle screen Call Command Effect DisplayOn() AFh Normal display DisplayOff() AEh Sleep; the RAM keeps its contents DisplayDim() ACh Dim mode, levels from the init table SetMasterCurrent() 87h Drive current scale, 0 to 15 The master current scales all three colours from 0 (dimmest) to 15 (brightest, the reset value). Lower brightness also slows the OLED's ageing. SetMasterCurrent() rejects values above 0x0F with Error::OutOfRange . Scroll ¶ // Horizontal scroll of all 64 rows by 1 column, no vertical offset, fastest interval (code 0). if ( ! display . ConfigureScroll ( 1 , 0 , 64 , 0 , 0 , true )) { // 2Eh, 27h, then 2Fh return false ; } // ... later: stop, and rewrite the display RAM from the frame. return display . StopScroll ( gfx ); // 2Eh, then Present(gfx) ConfigureScroll(h_offset, start_row, rows, v_offset, interval, activate) stops any running scroll ( 2Eh ), sends the SSD1331 scroll setup ( 27h ) and, with activate , starts it ( 2Fh ): the datasheet forbids changing the parameters while scrolling runs. The interval code is 0 to 3: a step every 6, 10, 100 or 200 frames. Stopping leaves the display RAM shifted, and the datasheet says to rewrite it: StopScroll(gfx) sends 2Eh and then Present(gfx) . StopScroll() without a context only sends 2Eh ; redraw yourself afterwards. Read the switch ¶ IsPressed() returns your port's GpioRead(CtrlPin::Switch) : the raw contact, with bounce. ButtonUI turns it into events: // Call every 10-20 ms from your loop; elapsed_ms is the time since the previous call. switch ( ui . Update ( display . IsPressed (), elapsed_ms )) { case isf15acp4 :: ButtonEvent :: Pressed : std :: printf ( "down, press #%lu 
 " , static_cast < unsigned long > ( ui . PressCount ())); break ; case isf15acp4 :: ButtonEvent :: Click : std :: printf ( "click 
 " ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: ButtonEvent :: LongPress : std :: printf ( "held 800 ms 
 " ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: ButtonEvent :: Released : std :: printf ( "released after a long press 
 " ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: ButtonEvent :: None : break ; } Event When Pressed The contact closed (counted in PressCount() ) Click Released before the long-press time LongPress Held for the long-press time (default 800 ms); reported once per press Released Released after a long press ButtonUI(debounce_ms, long_press_ms) defaults to 25 ms and 800 ms. It samples the contact once per debounce period, so call Update() more often than that. Handle errors ¶ if ( ! display . Initialize ()) { switch ( display . GetLastError ()) { case isf15acp4 :: Error :: NotInitialized : std :: printf ( "port: EnsureInitialized() failed 
 " ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: Error :: SpiWrite : std :: printf ( "port: WriteBytes() failed 
 " ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: Error :: InvalidParam : std :: printf ( "no port (null bus pointer) 
 " ); break ; default : std :: printf ( "error 0x%04x 
 " , display . GetErrorFlags ()); break ; } } if ( display . HasError ( isf15acp4 :: Error :: OutOfRange )) { // flags accumulate until cleared display . ClearErrorFlags ( static_cast < uint16_t > ( isf15acp4 :: Error :: OutOfRange )); } std :: printf ( "driver %s 
 " , Display :: GetDriverVersion ()); Error:: Set when SpiWrite Your Begin*() or WriteBytes() returned false NotInitialized EnsureInitialized() failed, or pixels before Initialize() InvalidParam No port, an odd pixel byte count, a wrong-size canvas OutOfRange A window off the panel, a master current above 15 GetLastError() is the most recent error; GetErrorFlags() is every error since the last ClearErrorFlags() . Error::GpioControl and Error::PowerSequence exist in the enum but nothing sets them yet. The display sends nothing back, so the driver cannot tell a missing or unpowered module from a working one: Troubleshooting starts there.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches the display. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application draws into a GraphicsContext and calls one SmartDisplay object, whose public calls (listed from inc/isf15acp4.hpp) initialise the SSD1331 controller, upload frames, run its hardware drawing commands and read the switch. Each call becomes command and data transactions. The communication interface (SpiInterface in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards them to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes SPI bytes with D/C and SS, sets the control pins, reads the switch and waits. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/isf15acp4.hpp SmartDisplay public calls ; inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer What You change it Hardware-agnostic core SmartDisplay<SpiType> and the graphics, animation and button helpers Never Communication interface SpiInterface<Derived> Never Platform port Your class Once per MCU or board ( Porting ) Everything above the port is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test port. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one call reaches the display ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant G as GraphicsContext participant D as SmartDisplay participant P as Your port A->>G: DrawString(4, 4, "READY", Green) G->>G: 5 x 7 glyphs into the RGB565 canvas A->>D: Present(gfx) D->>P: BeginCommand(), WriteBytes(15h 00h 5Fh), EndTransaction() D->>P: BeginCommand(), WriteBytes(75h 00h 3Fh), EndTransaction() D->>P: BeginData(), WriteBytes(frame, 12288), EndTransaction() P-->>D: true / false D-->>A: true / false The pieces of the core ¶ Type Owns SmartDisplay Reset and supply sequence, init table, windows, frame upload, hardware drawing, scroll, brightness, switch, errors GraphicsContext The drawing surface, with the backend chosen at construction Canvas A 96 x 64 RGB565 frame, software drawing, the 5 x 7 font Animator Frame timing; animations:: holds four built-in effects ButtonUI Switch debouncing and events, status and gauge drawing ssd1331:: Command opcodes, init tables, timing constants Types SmartDisplayConfig , ProductVariant , Error , Rect , Point , Color565 , colors:: Why CRTP ¶ The interface is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your port's methods directly and inlines them; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. The cost is that the driver type names the port: SmartDisplay<MySpi> . Its link back to the display in hardware-direct mode is a small table of function pointers ( DisplayPresenter ), so the graphics code does not depend on your port type. Memory ¶ Nothing is allocated on the heap. The large objects are the frames: Object Size Canvas 12,288 bytes (96 x 64 x 2), whatever the variant GraphicsContext One Canvas plus a few bytes, in every backend SmartDisplay A few dozen bytes; FillScreen() builds a temporary Canvas on the stack Keep a GraphicsContext as a static or long-lived object rather than on a small task stack, and give the task that calls FillScreen() at least 13 KB of stack. docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries marked BREAKING need source changes in code that used the affected API. Unreleased ¶ Breaking changes ¶ BREAKING CtrlPin::Reset now means "held in reset": Initialize() drives it Active for at least 3 µs, then Inactive , and leaves it Inactive (SSD1331 rev 1.2 section 7.9, Table 18). Map Active to the low RES# level, like ChipSelect . Ports that followed the earlier workaround ( Active = high) must invert their Reset mapping; the ESP32 example adapter already maps it this way. BREAKING Present() , DrawCanvas() and FillScreen() now send each pixel high byte first on every CPU (SSD1331 rev 1.2 section 7.5.2, Table 9). Remove any byte swap added around Present() as a workaround, or it swaps the frame back. BREAKING Pixel data ( Present() , DrawCanvas() , FillScreen() , DrawPixel() , WriteColors() ) is now converted from RGB565 to the panel's blue-green-red word, so red and blue are no longer swapped against the hardware line and rectangle commands (NKK Application Notes rev H section 9). Code that pre-swapped red and blue to compensate must stop. WritePixels() still sends raw bytes: convert them with ssd1331::ToPanelPixel() . Added ¶ SmartDisplay::WriteColors(colors, count) streams Color565 pixels in the controller's byte order. WritePixels() still sends raw bytes unchanged. SmartDisplay::StopScroll() stops hardware scrolling ( 2Eh ); StopScroll(gfx) also rewrites the display RAM with Present(gfx) , as the SSD1331 requires after 2Eh . ssd1331::ToPanelPixel(color) converts a Color565 to the panel's pixel word. Fixed ¶ The reset pulse left RES# low with an active-low port, so the controller stayed in reset. The driver now asserts RES# for at least 3 µs, releases it and waits 10 µs (reset completion is 2 µs maximum) before the first command. Frames went out in memory order, low byte first on little-endian MCUs (ESP32, Arm Cortex-M, x86), so colours were wrong after Present() . The canvas upload and the hardware-direct flush hook now serialise each pixel high byte first. Pixels drawn through the frame or DrawPixel() showed red as blue and blue as red: the NKK init tables select the normal colour order (A0h bit 2 = 0), in which the pixel word's high 5 bits are colour C, blue on these panels. DrawLine() and DrawRectangle() already sent red as colour A and were correct. ProductVariant::Isc15anp4 and Isc01p failed Initialize() with Error::OutOfRange : SetFullWindow() passed RAM addresses ( 10h .. 4Fh , 16h .. 49h ) to SetWindow() , which checks display coordinates. SetWindow() , DrawLine() , DrawRectangle() and ClearWindow() now take display coordinates and add the variant's RAM offset (NKK Application Notes rev H, Tables 4 and 5). With GraphicsBackend::HardwareDirect , Initialize() bound the display to a temporary context, so contexts from CreateGraphicsContext() drew into RAM and nothing reached the panel. CreateGraphicsContext() on a non-const display now returns a bound context; a const display still returns an unbound one. ConfigureScroll() sent new 27h parameters while scrolling could be running, and with activate = false sent 27h before 2Eh . It now always sends 2Eh first, then 27h , then 2Fh only when activating (SSD1331 rev 1.2 Table 10, 27h note 2). cmake --install produced an unusable package: the headers were installed without the src/*.ipp files they include, and the exported target was hf::hf_isf15acp4 instead of hf::isf15acp4 . Headers now install to include/hf_isf15acp4/inc/ , the .ipp files to include/hf_isf15acp4/src/ , and find_package(hf_isf15acp4) provides hf::isf15acp4 . Documentation ¶ The documentation site moved to the HardFOC MkDocs platform: new page set (quickstart, hardware, architecture, graphics, animations, API guide, configuration, porting, examples, troubleshooting), the Doxygen API reference under /api/ , and every code sample compiled by the host build from tests/docs/ . Corrected the hardware facts against the NKK datasheet: the ISC15ANP4 is 64 x 48 and the ISC01P 52 x 36 (not 96 x 64 and 128 x 128), VCC is 14 V to 16 V (15 V typical), the power sequence raises VCC after the reset pulse, and the panel's pixels are 0.222 mm x 0.293 mm. Removed the illustrations whose pinout and wiring did not match the part. Added ¶ Host unit tests ( HF_ISF15ACP4_BUILD_TESTS ) that run the driver against a recording SPI port.

docs.text: Graphics ¶ How drawing works: the graphics context and its three backends, colours, text, images and what a frame costs. Snippets on this page are compiled from tests/docs/graphics.cpp . The graphics context ¶ GraphicsContext is the surface your code draws on. display.CreateGraphicsContext() returns one with the display's variant and backend; you can also construct one directly with GraphicsContext(ProductVariant, GraphicsBackend) . Call Draws Clear() The whole frame SetPixel() , GetPixel() One pixel; out of range is ignored (reads black) DrawHLine() , DrawVLine() A row or column line, both ends included DrawRect() , FillRect() Outline or solid Rect{x0, y0, x1, y1} , inclusive DrawChar() , DrawString() 5 x 7 font on a background colour (default black) BlitRgb565() A row-major RGB565 image, clipped at the edge Every context holds a full 96 x 64 frame (12,288 bytes), so create one and keep it, rather than one per draw. Backends ¶ SmartDisplayConfig::graphics picks how a context behaves. It is fixed when the context is created. Backend Drawing Present() BuiltinCanvas Changes the frame in RAM Uploads it Animator The same; pair it with the Animator class Uploads it HardwareDirect Shapes go to the display at once Sends nothing BuiltinCanvas is the default. Hardware-direct drawing ¶ isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplay < MySpi > display ( & spi , isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplayConfig {. graphics = isf15acp4 :: GraphicsBackend :: HardwareDirect }); if ( ! display . Initialize ()) { return false ; } auto gfx = display . CreateGraphicsContext (); // already bound to this display gfx . FillRect ({ 8 , 8 , 87 , 55 }, colors :: Blue ); // sent at once as 26h / 22h gfx . DrawHLine ( 8 , 87 , 31 , colors :: White ); // sent at once as 21h return display . Present ( gfx ); // nothing to do: returns true What to know before choosing it: The context comes bound. display.CreateGraphicsContext() connects the context it returns to the display. A context you construct yourself, or get from a const display, needs display.ConfigurePresenter(gfx) . Keep the display alive as long as the context. Text and images stay in RAM. DrawChar() , DrawString() and BlitRgb565() draw into the context's frame, which Present() never sends in this mode. It saves no RAM. The context still holds a 12,288-byte frame, and Clear() becomes FillScreen() , which builds a second frame on the stack. Each pixel is a transaction. SetPixel() costs 8 bytes and three SS-low transactions. It suits a few lines and rectangles over whatever is on the screen. For anything with text, use the canvas. Colours ¶ Colours are Color565 : 16-bit RGB565, red in bits 15 to 11, green 10 to 5, blue 4 to 0. Helper Use MakeColor565(r, g, b) From 8-bit channels colors::Red ... Ten presets BmpPixelToColor565() From a 24-bit BMP pixel (B, G, R) The presets are Black , White , Red , Green , Blue , Yellow , Cyan , Magenta , Orange and Gray . The SSD1331 takes each pixel as two bytes, high byte first (65k-colour format, SSD1331 datasheet Table 9). Present() , DrawCanvas() , FillScreen() , DrawPixel() and WriteColors() send that order on any CPU, so the canvas stays in native byte order and needs no swapping. The panel stores each pixel as blue, green, red (blue in bits 15 to 11, red in 4 to 0; NKK application notes, section 9). The same calls convert every Color565 to that order with ssd1331::ToPanelPixel() , and the hardware line and rectangle commands send red as colour A and blue as colour C, so a colour looks the same however it is drawn. Only WritePixels() sends bytes unchanged: give it panel-order words. Text ¶ The font covers ASCII 32 (space) to 126 ( ~ ). Each character is 5 x 7 pixels with one column of spacing, so a line holds 16 characters and the panel 8 lines at a 8-pixel pitch. Characters outside that range are skipped (their cell is left as it was). Strings do not wrap; text past the right edge is clipped. Images ¶ Convert a PNG to a C++ array with scripts/convert_image_to_rgb565.py (needs Pillow): python3 scripts/convert_image_to_rgb565.py icon.png -o main/icon.hpp -n Icon -W 16 -H 16 It writes kIconWidth , kIconHeight and kIconRgb565 , resizing the image to -W x -H (default 96 x 64). Then blit it: // 16 x 16 RGB565 icon, row-major, from scripts/convert_image_to_rgb565.py. extern const isf15acp4 :: Color565 kIconRgb565 [ 16 * 16 ]; bool show_icon ( Display & display , isf15acp4 :: GraphicsContext & gfx ) { gfx . Clear ( colors :: Black ); gfx . BlitRgb565 ( 40 , 24 , 16 , 16 , kIconRgb565 ); // clipped at the frame edge return display . Present ( gfx ); } The panel's pixels are 1.32 times taller than wide, so a 96 x 64 image fills a 21.3 mm x 18.7 mm area. Draw artwork at that shape (about 96 : 84) and let the script squeeze it to 96 x 64, and circles stay round. What a frame costs ¶ Operation Bytes At 6 MHz Present() 12,294 16.4 ms Filled rectangle 17 23 µs DrawLine() 8 11 µs DrawPixel() 8 11 µs FillScreen() costs the same as Present() ; DrawPixel() also takes three SS-low transactions. Times are bytes x 8 / 6 MHz, before your port's per-transaction overhead and your drawing time. The SPI clock limits full-frame animation to about 60 frames a second; 25 to 30 is a comfortable target. Next: Animations runs frames on a timer.

docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and an ISF15ACP4, with which bus settings and supply sequence, and the limits to stay inside. All values here come from the NKK Frameless OLED Pushbutton datasheet (dated 10/03/19), and for the controller's command set from the Solomon Systech SSD1331 datasheet (Rev 1.2). When they disagree with your board's schematic, the schematic wins for pin numbers and levels. Pins ¶ Terminal numbers are not printed on the switch; take them from the footprint drawing in the datasheet. Pin Signal Function 1, 2 SW Switch contacts, normally open; closed while pressed 3 VDD Logic supply, 2.4 V to 3.5 V 4 SS SPI slave select, active low (input) 5 RES Reset, active low (input); low initialises the controller 6 D/C Low: the byte is a command; high: the byte is display data (input) 7 SCK SPI clock (input) 8 SDI SPI data in (input) 9 VCC OLED drive supply, 14 V to 16 V 10 GND Ground There is no data output: the display is written, never read. The switch is a separate contact pair; wire pin 1 to an MCU input with a pull-up and pin 2 to ground, and a press reads low. The driver names its control lines isf15acp4::CtrlPin : ChipSelect , DataCommand , Reset , VccEnable and Switch . VccEnable is not a module pin: it is the enable input of the supply that makes VCC. Bus settings ¶ Setting Value Mode SPI mode 0 (or 3): SDI is shifted in on the rising edge of SCK, MSB first Clock t cycle 150 ns minimum, so at most about 6.6 MHz; SCK high and low 75 ns minimum each Frame Bytes; D/C is sampled with the last bit of each byte Chip select SS setup 75 ns, SS hold 60 ns; keep SS low for a command and all its parameter bytes D/C Setup and hold 40 ns around the byte Data setup, hold 40 ns each SCK rise, fall 15 ns maximum The driver's constants are ssd1331::kMaxSpiClockHz (6,600,000) and ssd1331::kResetPulseMinUs (3). The ESP32 examples run at 6 MHz. Each driver call is one or more SS-low transactions: a command with its parameters (D/C low), or a block of pixel data (D/C high). sequenceDiagram participant H as Host (driver + port) participant D as ISF15ACP4 H->>D: SS low, D/C low: 15h 00h 5Fh (columns 0..95), SS high H->>D: SS low, D/C low: 75h 00h 3Fh (rows 0..63), SS high H->>D: SS low, D/C high: 12,288 bytes of RGB565 pixels, SS high Note over D: The address wraps inside the window: row by row Power ¶ Parameter VDD VCC Range 2.4 V to 3.5 V 14.0 V to 16.0 V Typical 2.8 V 15.0 V Absolute maximum 4.0 V 19.0 V All pixels on 0.17 mA (0.20 max) 11.0 mA (13.2 max) Asleep 10 µA max 10 µA max VDD feeds the logic and VCC the OLED drive. Currents are at 25 °C, VDD = 2.8 V, VCC = 15 V. Inputs swing from 0.2 x VDD (low, maximum) to 0.8 x VDD (high, minimum) and must stay within −0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V, so drive the module from MCU I/O at the same voltage as VDD. Power sequence ¶ The datasheet's power on / off sequence: Raise VDD with RES, SS, D/C, SCK and SDI low or high impedance. Hold RES low for at least 3 µs, then release it. Turn VCC on at least 3 µs later, then send the initialisation commands. To power off, send display off ( AEh ), turn VCC off, then VDD (0 µs minimum between them). While VCC is off it sits near VDD through the controller's ESD protection; that is expected. SmartDisplay::Initialize(true) does steps 2 and 3: it holds Reset active (RES low) for 3 µs, releases it, waits 10 µs, sets VccEnable active, waits 1 ms and sends the initialisation table. With Initialize(false) it leaves VCC alone, for boards that switch the supply themselves. The driver has no power-off call: send DisplayOff() , then drop VccEnable from your own code. Switch ¶ Parameter Value Circuit SPST, normally open, momentary Rating 100 mA at 12 V DC, resistive Contact resistance 200 mΩ maximum Operating force 2.0 N ± 0.5 N; never more than 100 N on the keytop Travel 1.8 mm Endurance 1,000,000 operations, mechanical and electrical The contacts bounce like any switch. ButtonUI debounces them ( API guide ). Display ¶ Parameter Value Pixels 96 x 64 RGB, passive matrix Viewing area 21.28 mm x 18.74 mm Pixel pitch 0.222 mm x 0.293 mm: pixels are taller than wide Colours 65,536 (16-bit, R5 G6 B5) or 256 (8-bit); the driver uses 16-bit Luminance 80 to 130 cd/m², 105 typical, white, all pixels on Life 50,000 h at 100 cd/m², 40 % of pixels on, 25 °C Temperature Operating −20 °C to +70 °C, storage −30 °C to +80 °C Because a pixel is 0.293 / 0.222 = 1.32 times taller than wide, artwork drawn on square pixels looks stretched vertically. Scale it to about 76 % of its height before converting it ( Graphics ). OLED pixels lose brightness with use, the busiest ones fastest. For a screen that stays the same for hours, move or invert it from time to time, dim it ( DisplayDim() , SetMasterCurrent() ) or turn it off. Product variants ¶ The driver carries initialisation tables for three NKK SmartDisplay parts with the same controller. This repository is tested only with the ISF15ACP4. ProductVariant Part Pixels Isf15acp4 Frameless pushbutton 96 x 64 Isc15anp4 OLED pushbutton 64 x 48 Isc01p OLED display 52 x 36 The two smaller parts show a window of the controller's 96 x 64 RAM that starts at column 16 ( 10h , ISC15ANP4) or 22 ( 16h , ISC01P), per the NKK application notes. Every driver call takes display coordinates, 0 to width - 1 and 0 to height - 1, and adds that offset itself. Mounting and handling ¶ The module is static sensitive: handle it at an ESD-safe bench. Keep the OLED below 80 °C when soldering (NKK soldering profile A); the socket AT9704-085L lets you fit the button after soldering and replace it in the field. NKK recommends series resistors and buffers on the signal lines against noise, and grounded bracket legs. Clean the keytop with a dry cloth; no solvents. docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-mostly C++20 library with one source file and no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 12+ or a current MSVC. The headers use designated initialisers. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns bool or a value. About 12.3 KB of RAM per graphics context, and 13 KB of stack if you call FillScreen() ( Architecture ). Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-isf15acp4-driver.git external/hf-isf15acp4-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-isf15acp4-driver Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-isf15acp4-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf_isf15acp4 ) The hf_isf15acp4 target (alias hf::isf15acp4 ) carries the include directories, including the generated version header, and requires C++20 ( cxx_std_20 ), so your target does not need to set either. Both options default to OFF : Option Effect when ON HF_ISF15ACP4_ENABLE_WARNINGS -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on the driver HF_ISF15ACP4_BUILD_TESTS The host tests in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ The root CMakeLists.txt installs the static library, the headers with the .ipp files they include and the generated version header, and a hf_isf15acp4Config.cmake package: cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build && cmake --install build --prefix /opt/hardfoc find_package ( hf_isf15acp4 1 REQUIRED CONFIG ) # CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/hardfoc target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::isf15acp4 ) The headers go to include/hf_isf15acp4/inc/ and the .ipp files to include/hf_isf15acp4/src/ , the same layout as the source tree; the target adds include/hf_isf15acp4/inc to your include path. The host test hf_isf15acp4_install_package installs into the build tree and builds a consumer against it. ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is examples/esp32/components/hf_isf15acp4/ . Copy that folder into your project's components/ (or point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it) and set the HF_ISF15ACP4_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout; the wrapper stops with a clear message when the path is wrong. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_isf15acp4 . The wrapper also brings the example's Kconfig menu ( Configuration ). Without a build system ¶ Add inc/ to the include path and compile src/isf15acp4_font_data.cpp . The .ipp files in src/ are included by the headers. Generate isf15acp4_version.h from inc/isf15acp4_version.h.in (CMake does this at configure time), or provide your own with the four HF_ISF15ACP4_VERSION_* macros. How the build is organised ¶ Layer Role Settings Sources, include directories, version: the single source of truth Library Static library for host builds and CI ESP-IDF Component wrapper over the same settings The version is set once in the settings file ( cmake/hf_isf15acp4_build_settings.cmake ) and written into isf15acp4_version.h at configure time. Read it at run time: const char * v = isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplay < MySpi >:: GetDriverVersion (); // "1.0.0" Next ¶ Quickstart wires the button and shows text; Porting writes the SPI interface for your MCU.

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the SPI interface. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls eight methods on a class you derive from isf15acp4::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp ). The base class uses CRTP: the calls are resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application draws into a GraphicsContext and calls one SmartDisplay object, whose public calls (listed from inc/isf15acp4.hpp) initialise the SSD1331 controller, upload frames, run its hardware drawing commands and read the switch. Each call becomes command and data transactions. The communication interface (SpiInterface in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards them to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes SPI bytes with D/C and SS, sets the control pins, reads the switch and waits. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/isf15acp4.hpp SmartDisplay public calls ; inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ Method Contract EnsureInitialized() Bring SPI and GPIOs up; true when ready, also on later calls BeginCommand() D/C low, then SS low: a command and its parameters follow BeginData() D/C high, then SS low: display data follows EndTransaction() SS high, after the last bit has left WriteBytes(data, len) Send len bytes (up to 12,288), blocking until sent GpioSet(pin, signal) Drive SS, D/C, RES or VCC enable Active / Inactive GpioRead(pin) true when Switch is pressed, else false DelayUs(us) Wait at least that long (the driver uses 3, 10 and 1000) All return bool except EndTransaction() , GpioSet() and DelayUs() , which return void . SPI port ¶ my_spi.hpp class MySpi : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // Your board's GPIO numbers. static constexpr int kCs = 10 , kDc = 13 , kRes = 14 , kVccEn = 9 , kSwitch = 8 ; bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kCs , true ); // SS idle high platform_gpio_write ( kVccEn , false ); // 15 V drive supply off until after reset return platform_spi_init (); } // D/C low = command, high = data; SS low for the whole transaction. bool BeginCommand () noexcept { return begin ( false ); } bool BeginData () noexcept { return begin ( true ); } void EndTransaction () noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kCs , true ); } // Must not return before the last bit is on the wire: SS rises right after. bool WriteBytes ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } void GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: Active ; switch ( pin ) { case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: ChipSelect : platform_gpio_write ( kCs , ! active ); break ; // SS active low case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: DataCommand : platform_gpio_write ( kDc , active ); break ; // high = data case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset : platform_gpio_write ( kRes , ! active ); break ; // RES# active low case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: VccEnable : platform_gpio_write ( kVccEn , active ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Switch : break ; // input only } } // The switch closes pins 1-2; wired to GND with a pull-up, pressed reads low. bool GpioRead ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin ) noexcept { return pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Switch && ! platform_gpio_read ( kSwitch ); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool begin ( bool data ) noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kDc , data ); platform_gpio_write ( kCs , false ); return true ; } }; Rules the transfer must follow: SPI mode 0 (mode 3 also meets the datasheet), MSB first, at most 6.6 MHz. One SS-low transaction per Begin / End pair. The driver calls WriteBytes() one or more times inside it (a command's opcode, then its parameters; a frame in chunks of up to 128 bytes); keep SS low across all of them. Blocking writes. WriteBytes() must not return while bytes are still queued: EndTransaction() raises SS right after it, and the display drops a byte cut short. With DMA, wait for completion. No MISO. The display has no data output; leave MISO unconnected or free for other devices. Return false only for a bus failure. The driver turns it into Error::SpiWrite . Control pins ¶ The driver addresses pins by name and abstract level. Your port decides the physical level: Pin Driver use Active is ChipSelect Inactive at start Low DataCommand Active at start High (data) Reset Active 3 µs, then Inactive Low (RES# held in reset) VccEnable Active after reset Supply on Switch Read by IsPressed() Pressed Reset follows the other pins: Active is the asserted level, which for RES# is low. Initialize() drives it Active for at least 3 µs, then Inactive (high), and waits 10 µs before the first command (SSD1331 power-on sequence, reset completion 2 µs maximum). Reference implementation ¶ The ESP32 examples use esp32_isf15acp4_spi_adapter.hpp : an ESP-IDF spi_master device in mode 0 with SS as a GPIO, spi_device_polling_transmit() for blocking writes, an input with pull-up for the switch and esp_rom_delay_us() / vTaskDelay() for delays. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Check your port ¶ Build it: the port on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over it. With a logic analyser on SS, D/C and SCK, call Initialize() : you should see 21 command transactions (the init table) and two window commands, each with SS low around its bytes, and RES high at the end. Call FillScreen(isf15acp4::colors::White) , then FillScreen(isf15acp4::colors::Black) : the whole panel turns white, then dark. (White and black do not depend on byte order; for colours see Troubleshooting .) Read IsPressed() with the button held and released. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each display one owner task, or guard every call on a driver object (and its port) with one mutex. Several displays on one SPI bus need a separate SS per display, and the bus must not be used by another device between a Begin*() and its EndTransaction() .

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Show text on an ISF15ACP4 from your MCU: wire seven signals and two supplies, write a small port class, call four driver functions. The 15 V drive supply comes last Switch VCC (14 V to 16 V) with a GPIO-controlled supply or charge pump that is off at power-up. The datasheet turns it on only after VDD is up and the reset pulse is done, and off before VDD. A VCC that is always on skips that sequence. 1. Wire it ¶ MCU ISF15ACP4 pin Notes SPI MOSI 8 SDI Write only: the display has no data output SPI SCK 7 SCK SPI mode 0, up to 6.6 MHz; start at 1 MHz GPIO out 4 SS Chip select, active low; the port drives it GPIO out 6 D/C Low: command bytes; high: pixel data GPIO out 5 RES Reset, active low GPIO out VCC supply enable Turns on the 15 V supply that feeds pin 9 GPIO in, pull-up 1 SW Pin 2 SW to GND: pressed reads low 2.8 V or 3.3 V 3 VDD 2.4 V to 3.5 V; MCU I/O at the same level GND 10 GND Common ground for both supplies The Hardware page has the timing, the power sequence and the electrical limits. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the hf_isf15acp4 CMake target (or include inc/ and compile src/isf15acp4_font_data.cpp with C++20). Installation covers CMake and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-isf15acp4-driver.git external/hf-isf15acp4-driver 3. Write the port ¶ The port is the only platform code. It writes SPI bytes inside an SS-low transaction with D/C set, drives the control pins and waits. Replace the platform_* calls with your SDK's. my_spi.hpp class MySpi : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // Your board's GPIO numbers. static constexpr int kCs = 10 , kDc = 13 , kRes = 14 , kVccEn = 9 , kSwitch = 8 ; bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kCs , true ); // SS idle high platform_gpio_write ( kVccEn , false ); // 15 V drive supply off until after reset return platform_spi_init (); } // D/C low = command, high = data; SS low for the whole transaction. bool BeginCommand () noexcept { return begin ( false ); } bool BeginData () noexcept { return begin ( true ); } void EndTransaction () noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kCs , true ); } // Must not return before the last bit is on the wire: SS rises right after. bool WriteBytes ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } void GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: Active ; switch ( pin ) { case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: ChipSelect : platform_gpio_write ( kCs , ! active ); break ; // SS active low case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: DataCommand : platform_gpio_write ( kDc , active ); break ; // high = data case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset : platform_gpio_write ( kRes , ! active ); break ; // RES# active low case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: VccEnable : platform_gpio_write ( kVccEn , active ); break ; case isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Switch : break ; // input only } } // The switch closes pins 1-2; wired to GND with a pull-up, pressed reads low. bool GpioRead ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin ) noexcept { return pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Switch && ! platform_gpio_read ( kSwitch ); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool begin ( bool data ) noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kDc , data ); platform_gpio_write ( kCs , false ); return true ; } }; CtrlPin::Reset is active low like SS: Active holds the controller in reset, Inactive lets it run. Porting explains each method and the pin levels. 4. Show something ¶ main.cpp #include "isf15acp4.hpp" int show_ready ( MySpi & spi ) { isf15acp4 :: SmartDisplay < MySpi > display ( & spi ); // ISF15ACP4, software canvas if ( ! display . Initialize ()) { // 1. reset, 15 V on, SSD1331 init table return -1 ; // wiring, VCC or SPI: see GetLastError() } auto gfx = display . CreateGraphicsContext (); // 2. draw into a 96 x 64 RGB565 frame gfx . Clear ( isf15acp4 :: colors :: Black ); gfx . DrawString ( 4 , 4 , "READY" , isf15acp4 :: colors :: Green ); gfx . DrawRect ({ 0 , 0 , 95 , 63 }, isf15acp4 :: colors :: White ); if ( ! display . Present ( gfx )) { // 3. send the frame (12,288 bytes) return -2 ; } return display . IsPressed () ? 1 : 0 ; // 4. the switch, through your port } What each step does: Initialize() calls your EnsureInitialized() , pulses RES for at least 3 µs, enables VCC, waits 1 ms, sends the ISF15ACP4 initialisation table (which ends with display on) and sets the full 96 x 64 window. Nothing else works until it returns true . CreateGraphicsContext() returns a canvas the size of the panel. Drawing only changes RAM on your MCU. Present() streams the frame to the display: 12,288 bytes with D/C high. IsPressed() calls your GpioRead(CtrlPin::Switch) . This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. If it does not work ¶ Symptom First thing to check Initialize() returns false GetLastError() : your EnsureInitialized() or WriteBytes() failed Returns true , screen stays dark RES ends low ( Reset mapping inverted), VCC not at 14 V to 16 V, SS or D/C swapped Shapes in the right place, colours wrong A leftover byte swap or raw WritePixels() bytes ( Troubleshooting ) Switch always pressed or never Pull-up on the SW pin, active level in GpioRead() Next ¶ API guide : brightness, hardware drawing, raw pixel writes, the switch, errors. docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host unit tests against a recording port, compiled documentation, ESP32 builds and static analysis, on every pull request. Host unit tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a port that records every SS-low transaction (D/C level and bytes), every control-pin change and every delay, on a virtual clock. They check the exact SSD1331 byte stream, the reset and VCC sequence, and the error flags, without hardware. cmake -S . -B build-host -DHF_ISF15ACP4_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_driver.cpp Init table and window for each variant, reset timing, VCC, port failures, range checks, pixel byte and colour order, hardware commands, frame upload, hardware-direct binding, scrolling, canvas, ButtonUI , Animator tests/mock_spi.hpp The recording port, with fault injection tests/test_harness.hpp A dependency-free test registry and CHECK macros tests/install_consumer/ CTest hf_isf15acp4_install_package : installs the package into the build tree and builds a find_package() consumer The display returns no data, so the tests check what the driver sends, not what the panel shows. Colours and pixel order need a look at real hardware. Documentation snippets ¶ Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target hf_isf15acp4_doc_snippets ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. A change to the API that breaks a page breaks the build first. CI workflows ¶ Workflow What it checks Host unit tests GCC and Clang build and run the tests and the doc snippets ESP32 examples build Every app in examples/esp32/app_config.yml , for each listed ESP-IDF version and build type C++ lint, C++ analysis clang-format, clang-tidy and cppcheck Docs Strict site build, figure and generated-table drift, Doxygen, link check, Lighthouse budget Markdown lint, YAML lint, link check Repository text files The workflows call the shared, versioned workflows of hf-general-ci-tools and hf-espidf-ci-tools . On hardware ¶ The ESP32 examples are the hardware test suite: isf15acp4_comprehensive_test runs every driver call and prints a pass / fail summary over the serial monitor. It sees only the return values; check the panel by eye.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up an ISF15ACP4, their causes and the fix for each, cheapest check first. The display sends nothing back, so the driver cannot see a wiring or supply fault: Initialize() returns true as long as your port's calls succeed. A logic analyser on SS, D/C, SCK, SDI and RES, and a meter on VCC, answer most questions in minutes. Screen stays dark after Initialize() returns true ¶ Check Fix RES is low after Initialize() Map Reset Active to low, Inactive to high ( Porting ) VCC (pin 9) is not 14 V to 16 V VccEnable mapping, your supply's enable level, Initialize(true) D/C is high during the init table BeginCommand() must set D/C low SS rises between an opcode and its parameters One SS-low transaction per Begin / End pair SCK above 6.6 MHz, or not mode 0 Lower the clock; 1 MHz for bring-up Pins numbered from the part Numbers are not printed on it: use the datasheet's footprint drawing Initialize() returns false ¶ GetLastError() says which part failed: Error Cause NotInitialized Your EnsureInitialized() returned false : the SPI bus or GPIO set-up failed SpiWrite BeginCommand() or WriteBytes() returned false InvalidParam The driver was constructed with a null port pointer OutOfRange A window outside the visible area: see the next section Initialize() fails with OutOfRange ¶ SetWindow() takes display coordinates and rejects a rectangle that goes past the variant's visible area (96 x 64, 64 x 48 or 52 x 36). Do not add the ISC15ANP4 or ISC01P column offset yourself: the driver does ( Hardware ). Colours wrong after Present() ¶ Shapes and text are in the right place but the colours are not. The driver sends each pixel high byte first on any CPU, so check your own code: Remove any byte swap added around Present() for earlier releases: it now swaps the frame back. WritePixels() sends your bytes unchanged. For Color565 buffers use WriteColors() ( API guide ). Red and blue swapped ¶ The panel stores pixels as blue, green, red, and the driver converts every Color565 it sends. If red shows as blue in one kind of drawing only, check: Raw WritePixels() bytes: they go out unchanged, so convert each colour with ssd1331::ToPanelPixel() or use WriteColors() . A remap value ( A0h ) changed from the NKK initialisation table: bit 2 selects the colour order. Keep the table's value. docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Three layers, one of them yours ¶ Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application draws into a GraphicsContext and calls one SmartDisplay object, whose public calls (listed from inc/isf15acp4.hpp) initialise the SSD1331 controller, upload frames, run its hardware drawing commands and read the switch. Each call becomes command and data transactions. The communication interface (SpiInterface in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards them to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes SPI bytes with D/C and SS, sets the control pins, reads the switch and waits. Below it is the hardware.
